section_summary: This section follows the dispute over Japan’s requirement that oil companies store six months’ supply under the Petroleum Industry Law. American and British companies resist the cost, consider offering coal hydrogenation technology in exchange for the earlier five-point arrangement, and face proposed tariffs they say favor Japanese refiners. State Department and embassy correspondence records diplomatic discussions, company proposals, and Japan’s refusal to treat hydrogenation as a substitute for storage.

people.name: Stanley K. Hornbeck
people.role: Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs

people.name: Edwin L. Neville
people.role: U.S. Chargé d’Affaires ad interim in Tokyo

people.name: Yoshino
people.role: Japanese Vice Minister for Commerce and Industry

people.name: Shinichi Kojima
people.role: Head of the Japanese Mining Bureau

people.name: Sakai
people.role: Chief of the Japanese Fuel Section

people.name: Kurusu
people.role: Chief of the Japanese Foreign Office Bureau of Commercial Affairs

people.name: T. G. Ely
people.role: Managing Director, Rising Sun Petroleum Company

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Ickes memorandum on oil exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Hull acknowledges and returns Ickes’s memorandum on oil exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hull suggests that the Secretaries of War and the Navy also read it.

subfiles.title: Conversation with British Embassy about Japanese oil storage
subfiles.about: British and American officials discuss possible joint representations against Japan’s six-month oil storage requirement.
subfiles.summary: Broadmead asks whether Washington would act with the British Embassy in Tokyo. Mackay expresses willingness to consider a legal or treaty basis, while noting uncertainty about the value of further representations.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation forwarded to London
subfiles.about: The Department forwards the British Embassy conversation memorandum.
subfiles.summary: Transmits the November 22 conversation for information.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation forwarded to Tokyo
subfiles.to: American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Department forwards the British Embassy conversation memorandum.
subfiles.summary: Transmits the November 22 conversation for information.

subfiles.title: File note on Tokyo despatch No. 1554
subfiles.about: A reviewer recommends reading Tokyo’s despatch on the oil situation.
subfiles.summary: The despatch adds little to an earlier telegram but merits reading in full.

subfiles.title: American oil interests in Japan
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Neville reports Japan’s insistence on six months of oil stocks and demands a decision from foreign companies.
subfiles.summary: Japanese officials say the five-point memorandum did not promise a change in law and offer compensation instead. They seek an early answer on compliance. Neville concludes that the companies now face the decisive choice and sees little scope for further diplomacy.

subfiles.title: Notes of meeting at Department of Commerce and Industry
subfiles.about: Japanese officials tell foreign oil representatives that the storage obligation cannot be negotiated.
subfiles.summary: Yoshino and Kurusu distinguish the five-point memorandum from a binding promise. They explain postponed enforcement and proposed compensation, request the companies’ decision, and discuss quotas and prices.

subfiles.title: Kojima letter on six-month oil stocks
subfiles.about: Kojima confirms that Japan will not modify the six-month stock requirement.
subfiles.summary: He says enforcement was extended but companies must comply with the law.

subfiles.title: Tokyo oil despatches forwarded to London
subfiles.about: The Department sends Tokyo despatches on Japan’s oil situation.
subfiles.summary: Forwards despatches and enclosures for the ambassador’s information.

subfiles.title: Telephone conversation with Parker on oil policy
subfiles.about: Hornbeck asks Standard-Vacuum to decide what position would support further diplomatic representations.
subfiles.summary: He describes embassy support for renewed representations but says the companies must clarify whether they could withdraw or cannot afford six months’ stocks.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram No. 240 on proposed hydrogenation offer
subfiles.about: Oil companies propose trading coal hydrogenation assistance for adherence to the five-point memorandum.
subfiles.summary: Neville describes the companies’ planned letter, possible approach to Mitsui, and proposed British and American diplomatic contacts.

subfiles.title: Authorization for limited Tokyo representations
subfiles.about: The Department authorizes coordinated representations while distancing itself from the companies’ hydrogenation proposal.
subfiles.summary: The embassy must avoid implying U.S. government support for the commercial offer.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to despatch No. 1542
subfiles.about: A file note directs readers to a despatch on oil interests and monopoly.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references despatch No. 1542 in another file.

subfiles.title: Extract on gasoline price increase
subfiles.about: The extract reports a gasoline price increase and the foreign companies’ response.
subfiles.summary: Japan sanctioned a 2½-sen gasoline price increase. Company directors still expected the authorities to honor the April five-point program.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck memorandum on December 11 call with Parker
subfiles.about: Hornbeck discusses the companies’ hydrogenation proposal and limits on embassy participation.
subfiles.summary: Parker authorizes consultation with the War and Navy Departments. Hornbeck advises that Tokyo’s embassy should report developments before taking action with Japanese authorities.

subfiles.title: Statement read to Parker about hydrogenation proposal
subfiles.about: The Department sets out reservations about the companies’ proposed offer of coal hydrogenation technology.
subfiles.summary: The statement insists that the commercial proposal remain the companies’ responsibility, questions its likely effect, and comments on proposed approaches to Japanese officials and Mitsui.

subfiles.title: Further telephone conversation with Parker
subfiles.about: Parker seeks embassy action following Tokyo’s telegram No. 240.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck says the Department will consider the requested instruction but cannot be associated with the hydrogenation offer.

subfiles.title: Parker memoranda forwarded to Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Department forwards two memoranda on conversations with Parker.
subfiles.summary: Transmits the December 13 memoranda for information.

subfiles.title: Parker memoranda forwarded to London
subfiles.about: The Department forwards two memoranda on conversations with Parker.
subfiles.summary: Transmits the December 13 memoranda for information.

subfiles.title: Parker letter enclosing proposed oil policy messages
subfiles.about: Parker sends British and American company messages concerning the proposed hydrogenation offer.
subfiles.summary: He asks whether the U.S. government can help arrange introductions to Japanese naval or military officials.

subfiles.title: London proposal for telegram to Yokohama
subfiles.about: British interests propose rejecting extra storage investment and offering a coal liquefaction license.
subfiles.summary: The draft argues that compensation and annual quotas cannot justify the six-month requirement. It proposes hydrogenation technology in return for the five-point arrangement and considers Mitsui’s role.

subfiles.title: Draft cable to Agnew in London
subfiles.about: Standard-Vacuum proposes instructions for offering hydrogenation assistance to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The draft suggests involving Mitsui and possibly the embassies. It also warns that reduced quotas and tariffs could progressively diminish the foreign companies’ Japanese trade.

subfiles.title: Parker letter enclosing cable sent to Yokohama
subfiles.about: Parker reports revised company instructions sent to Yokohama.
subfiles.summary: The revision limits the local representatives’ authority to discussions while the companies consider their next move.

subfiles.title: Standard-Vacuum cable from New York to Yokohama
subfiles.about: The company instructs its Japanese representatives on proposing hydrogenation assistance.
subfiles.summary: Despite damaged text, the cable directs discussion of patent and technical help for making oil from coal in exchange for the five-point arrangement. It suggests consulting Mitsui.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Parker’s December letters
subfiles.about: Hornbeck acknowledges receipt of Parker’s letters and enclosures on Japan’s oil situation.
subfiles.summary: A brief acknowledgment for the record.

subfiles.title: File memorandum on Tokyo telegram No. 246
subfiles.about: A reviewer assesses Neville’s description of company intentions and the coordination of embassy efforts.
subfiles.summary: The note finds Neville’s statement about inability to trade too categorical but recommends allowing Grew’s planned informal approach.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram No. 246 on Japanese response
subfiles.about: Grew reports Japanese concern that foreign oil companies may withdraw.
subfiles.summary: Kurusu says the companies’ position has disturbed Commerce and Industry. The British ambassador has raised the question with Japan’s foreign minister; Grew plans to do so when another occasion arises.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram No. 251 on rejection of hydrogenation exchange
subfiles.about: Japan rejects treating coal liquefaction as a substitute for six-month oil stocks.
subfiles.summary: Officials say the five-point memorandum is nonbinding and warn of penalties and reduced quotas for noncompliance.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram No. 253 on possible guarantees
subfiles.about: Kurusu explores quota and price guarantees or Japanese capital as ways past the storage impasse.
subfiles.summary: He will pursue the question after January 7.

subfiles.title: Legal note on proposed petroleum tariff
subfiles.about: A reviewer assesses whether the proposed tariff supports an American discrimination protest.
subfiles.summary: The note finds no shown legal discrimination against foreign refining operations in Japan.

subfiles.title: Summary of Tokyo despatch No. 1590
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes proposed petroleum tariffs and the companies’ hydrogenation proposal.
subfiles.summary: It explains how the tariff calculation may favor refiners over importers, recounts the weakening of the five-point arrangement, and notes Japan’s refusal to connect coal liquefaction with the storage rule.

subfiles.title: American oil interests in Japan
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, U.S. Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Neville reports proposed tariff increases and renewed conflict over oil stockholding.
subfiles.summary: The companies say the gasoline and lubricant tariffs place greater burdens on imported refined products than on Japanese refiners. Japanese officials press for a stockholding decision and appear to disclaim the five-point memorandum. The companies propose a coal hydrogenation license in exchange for the earlier arrangement, although embassy observers doubt Japan will accept.

subfiles.title: Dickover conversation with MacGregor
subfiles.about: MacGregor alleges that Japan’s tariff policy aims to remove foreign firms from domestic oil distribution.
subfiles.summary: He argues that the proposed tariff favors refiners and would return foreign importers to losses, leaving Japanese firms to handle retail trade.

subfiles.title: London cable to Rising Sun Petroleum, Yokohama
subfiles.about: London directors reject extra oil storage investment and propose a hydrogenation license.
subfiles.summary: They cite uncertain compensation, annual quotas, and requisition rules. They authorize consideration of a coal hydrogenation offer, possibly involving Mitsui, in exchange for the five-point arrangement.

subfiles.title: New York cable to Standard-Vacuum, Yokohama
subfiles.about: New York authorizes a proposed hydrogenation exchange with the Japanese government.
subfiles.summary: The cable outlines patent and technical assistance, possible consultation with Mitsui, and discretion over an acceptance deadline.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1590 forwarded to London
subfiles.about: The Department forwards Neville’s despatch and enclosures on Japan’s oil situation.
subfiles.summary: Transmits despatch No. 1590 for information.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to gasoline reserves in North China
subfiles.about: A file note directs readers to a report on Japanese and Chinese gasoline reserves.
subfiles.summary: Cross-references despatch No. 1594 in another file.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram on Grew’s representations
subfiles.about: Grew raises the oil companies’ difficulties with Japan’s Vice Minister for Foreign Affairs.
subfiles.summary: The vice minister says Japan does not intend to deny foreign companies a reasonable return.

subfiles.title: Parker letter enclosing Yokohama cable
subfiles.about: Parker forwards a cable from Yokohama and promises further updates.
subfiles.summary: He expects no company decision until the following week.

subfiles.title: Yokohama cable on Japanese oil storage response
subfiles.about: The cable reports Japan’s refusal to replace stockholding with hydrogenation and warns of quota effects.
subfiles.summary: Officials maintain the six-month rule and say hydrogenation cannot substitute for it. The cable reports quarterly quotas favoring compliant Japanese firms and a possible discussion with Kurusu.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Parker’s December 24 letter
subfiles.about: Hornbeck acknowledges Parker’s letter and cable about recent oil developments.
subfiles.summary: He thanks Parker for the update and reciprocates his holiday greetings.
